questions.question: Compute `3^4 mod 7` by hand.
options: 1, since 81 = 11·7 + 4 then reduced once more
5, since 81 = 10·7 + 11 wraps once
6, since 81 mod 7 lands one below the modulus

questions.question: Why would you compute `a^k mod n` instead of `(a^k) mod n` separately?
options: To avoid floating-point error in intermediate exponentiations
To keep intermediates bounded; a^k itself can have billions of digits
To make the result fit into a fixed 32-bit integer representation
To ensure the result is always positive regardless of sign of a
questions.explanation: For RSA k ≈ 2^2048, so a^k would have ~10^617 digits. Reducing each step keeps multiplicands bounded by n².

questions.question: Square-and-multiply computes `a^k mod n` in how many multiplications?
options: Linear in k, requiring one multiplication per increment of k
Logarithmic in k, roughly 2·log₂(k) multiplications total
Constant in k once a precomputed window table exists for n
Quadratic in the bit length of k due to repeated squaring loops
questions.explanation: Each bit of k contributes one squaring; set bits also contribute one multiply. Total ~2·log₂(k) multiplications mod n.

questions.question: How does the Extended Euclidean method find `a⁻¹ mod n`?
options: Compute (s, t) with s·a + t·n = gcd(a,n)=1; then a⁻¹ ≡ s (mod n)
Compute a^φ(n) mod n via Euler; the result equals a⁻¹ for any a
Run Miller-Rabin on n until a primality witness gives the inverse
Take s = n − a so that s·a wraps to 1 modulo n in one step
questions.explanation: EEA returns Bezout (s, t) with s·a + t·n = 1. Reducing mod n: s·a ≡ 1 (mod n), so s ≡ a⁻¹.

questions.question: Fermat's-method inverse computes `a⁻¹ mod p` (for prime p) as which expression?
options: a^(p−1) mod p, then divided by p−1 to normalize the residue
a^(p−2) mod p, since a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) implies a · a^(p−2) ≡ 1
(p − a) mod p, exploiting the negation rule for prime moduli
a · (p−1) mod p, scaling by the order of the multiplicative group
questions.explanation: FLT: a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Multiplying both sides by a⁻¹ gives a⁻¹ ≡ a^(p−2) (mod p). Constant-time when p is fixed.

questions.question: Why is Python's built-in `pow(a, k, n)` preferred over a hand-rolled `mod_pow` in production?
options: Because it is GMP-backed and constant-time-aware for cryptographic use
Because it caches results across invocations using a global LRU table
Because it always returns a canonical signed representative in (−n/2, n/2]
Because it ignores the exponent when smaller than the modulus n
questions.explanation: CPython's `pow(a, k, n)` uses GMP / mpz_powm, which is highly optimized and uses sliding-window exponentiation. Cryptographic libraries also expose constant-time variants.

questions.question: A naive RSA decryption uses textbook square-and-multiply where each multiplication is timed differently for set vs cleared bits of `d`. What attack does this enable?
options: Wiener's attack, recovering d from a small public exponent estimate
Timing side channel: bit-by-bit recovery of d from decryption latency
Common-modulus attack, exploiting two parties sharing the modulus n
Hastad broadcast, exploiting low public exponent across many recipients
questions.explanation: If multiply runs only on set bits of d, latency reveals d's Hamming pattern. Constant-time exponentiation (Montgomery ladder, always-multiply) closes the channel.
